text:
Moth and Gravel. Field Note 11.
A model needs a place. An AI

narrated edition of the
published note. A small shrine

looks promising on the
workbench. It has a shape, a

palette, and a base. Turn it
around, and there is something

pleasing to look at from the
other side too. Now give it a

place on the island. Where does
it meet the ground? What can

stand in front of it? When
someone points at its roof, what

do they select? The object has
acquired neighbors. That changes

the questions. Keep a way back
to the material. Sky Stack

Builders Blender experiments
keep the editable model beside

its exported geometry. Checks
follow its size, origin,

surfaces and materials through
that journey. Those details have

a practical purpose. An object
should arrive at the size we

meant, with its base where we
expect it. If it doesn't, there

should be a way back to the
material that made it. The

generation script keeps existing
revisions rather than silently

replacing them. An earlier
attempt remains available to

return to, compare, or try
differently. Looking becomes

doing. A separate native pilot
draws real mesh geometry and

gives it a small set of
controls. Orbit, zoom, recenter,

and select. A click and the
beginning of a drag can look

much alike. The pilot gives them
a boundary. A small click

selects. Moving far enough
begins an orbit. Losing focus or

mouse capture clears the
gesture. That is a modest detail

with a large place in the
experience. Someone came to

choose an object. The view
should not move away from them

by accident. Someone came to
look around. The object should

not be selected merely because
that movement began over it. The

model is becoming something a
person can act upon. Give it

neighbors. From material to a
place in the world. The final

boundary marks work still to
investigate. The diagram does

not show completed gameplay
adoption. Open the full size

diagram. The shrine's asset
checks and the pilot's mesh

scene are separate pieces of
work. Together, they give us

useful material for the next
experiment. They do not yet show

the shrine living among the
game's terrain, weather, and

characters. A roof that is easy
to select alone may become

awkward beside a taller block. A
base that looks settled on an

empty grid may float above a
slope. Put several copies

together, and their silhouettes
may stop feeling distinct. These

are questions about the object
in company. Try one place

properly. The next study would
choose one asset and one use for

it. Put it somewhere the player
has a reason to visit. Look from

both sides and from above. Try
selecting it with a neighbor in

the way. Ask what the object
seems to be for and what the

person expects to happen when
they choose it. Observe the

scene's performance as well as
its appearance. Keep the earlier

representation available for
comparison. A beautiful model is

a beginning. There is another
kind of satisfaction in finding

where it belongs. Study scope,
source reading. Material on the

workbench. This study reads the
Blender Generation Root, a

committed shrine verification
record, and the separate native

mesh pilot's documentation. It
does not establish that the

shrine is part of the default
playable scene. The cover is

editorial artwork, and the
diagram is a schematic. No new

Blender render, pilot session,
gameplay capture, or performance

measurement was made for this
note. The proposed study of the

object among its neighbors
remains to be done.

You have been listening to Moth
and Gravel Field Notes. The

written edition is at
mothandgravel.com.
